What does Manton say is required for a person to attain true blessedness?

Manton teaches that true blessedness is attained only when the teaching of God prevails upon the heart and completely fills it, and that seeking blessedness in temporal things is a serious error. He warns that "It is not only an affront put upon God, but also a great wrong, to neglect the word of God, and the way he prescribes, and to seek blessedness in temporal things." Moreover, he explains that "That which fills must be greater than the thing filled," indicating that only the infinite fullness of God can satisfy the chaotic desires of the human heart. [Manton — Works Vol06]

What does Sibbes say about the role of constant, strong, and growing desires in confirming a sanctified soul?

Sibbes teaches that when a person’s desires are constant and ever‑increasing, they serve as evidence of a sanctified frame of soul and a new creature. He explains that such desires are not fleeting like a torrent but are perpetual, and they " Strong and growing desires argue the truth of desires ; as indeed a child of God hath never grace enough, never i^ith enough, never love enough, or comfort enough, till he come to heaven, ihey are growing desires more and more." In this view, holy desires spring from a holy soul and point toward the ultimate fulfillment of all promises in heaven. [Sibbes — Works Vol06]

What does Richard Mather say true joining to the church involves, as opposed to merely hearing the Word or having affection for the congregation?

Richard Mather teaches that true joining to the church is not simply dwelling in the town, hearing the Word, or expressing affection, but requires a voluntary covenantal fellowship. He explains that “it must be meant of joyning in that neere relation of Church-fellowship amongst them, so as to be engaged by volun tary consent and agreement to be members of their Church.” Thus, genuine membership is grounded in a conscious, covenantal agreement rather than mere attendance or emotional approval. [Richard Mather — Church Covenant]

What metaphor does Flavel recommend for describing the church’s deliverance, and how does he illustrate it with natural imagery?

Flavel teaches that believers should favor metaphors that the Spirit has authorized in Scripture, using the image of spring to portray the church’s deliverance. He writes, "In the spring, the earth, Hke a most bountiful parent, opens her bosom, produces variety of herbs, adorns the meadows with abundance of flowers ;" to show how nature’s renewal reflects the joy and freedom God brings to His people. [Flavel — Works Vol04]

What reason does Thomas Gouge give for believers to give alms of their possessions?

Thomas Gouge teaches that believers should give alms because doing so makes all things clean and sanctified for them. He writes, "Give alms of such things as you have, and behold all things are clean unto you:" and argues that this act aligns with the apostolic inference that charitable giving secures and sanctifies the rest of one's goods. Moreover, Gouge stresses that people are "Stewards, than Lords and Owners of this worlds goods; all is the Lords," so giving alms reflects proper stewardship and brings God's blessing. [Thomas Gouge — Surest And Safest Way Of Thriving]

According to Sibbes in Works Vol04, how should a person's particular calling relate to their love for God?

Sibbes teaches that love of God must be expressed through the specific duties and offices each person holds, not as an abstract feeling. He writes that the command to love God "must love God ' with all our mind^ with all our heart, with all our power and strength,' Deut. vi. 5 ; that is, in our particular places" applies to each individual’s role, whether magistrate, minister, or statesman, so that love is demonstrated in the performance of those responsibilities. Sibbes further asks, "How far doth thy activity, thy power, thy sphere, that thou canst do anj'thing, stretch ? So far must thy love ; and thou must shew thy love in all the powers and abilities that God hath fur'- nished thee with," emphasizing that love to God is discovered in action within one's calling. [Sibbes — Works Vol04]
